title: Quantum Behavior
note: Original lecture written in the style of Feynman's Caltech lectures. Not a transcript; to be replaced by the real recording of lecture #37 (4/3/62).

lines: Today we're going to talk about how very small things behave.
And I'll warn you right at the start: they don't behave like anything you've ever seen.
Not like little billiard balls. Not like waves on a pond. Not like springs, or clouds, or anything else.
So you're going to have to put up with that.
I can't explain it to you in terms of something familiar, because there isn't anything familiar.
What I can do is tell you exactly what happens. And then you'll know as much as anybody.
Let's start with an experiment we understand. Bullets.
We have a gun that sprays bullets in all directions, not very accurately.
In front of it there's an armor plate with two holes in it.
And behind that, a backstop, with a little box that catches bullets, and we can slide that box up and down.
We count how many bullets land in the box at each position. That gives us a probability.
Now, bullets come in lumps. You get one bullet or two bullets. You never get half a bullet.
If we close hole two, we get a curve from hole one alone. Call it P one.
Close hole one, we get P two.
Open both, and what do you get? Well, you just add them up. P one plus P two.
Every bullet went through one hole or the other. Nothing strange. Good.
Now let's do the same thing with water waves.
A little thing bobbing up and down in a pool makes circular waves.
Same wall, same two holes. Each hole now acts like a new source of waves.
Instead of a box catching bullets, we measure how much the water jiggles. The intensity.
And the intensity can be any size at all. It doesn't come in lumps.
With one hole open, we get a nice smooth bump, just like before.
But with both holes open, we get this: big, small, big, small.
At some places the two waves arrive in step and help each other.
At other places one is going up while the other is going down, and they cancel.
That's interference. And notice: the answer is not I one plus I two.
You have to add the heights of the waves first, and then square. The cross term is the interference.
Now we do it with electrons.
An electron gun: a hot wire and a little voltage. Same wall, same two holes.
For a detector we put a little counter that goes click when an electron hits it.
And here's the first thing. The clicks are all the same size. Click. Click. Click.
Never half a click. So electrons come in lumps, like bullets.
Turn the gun down very low, and still each click is a whole electron.
So we move the counter around, and we count clicks, and we make our curve.
And what do we get? Big, small, big, small. The wave pattern.
Lumps when they arrive, but they add up with interference. Like waves.
That should bother you. It bothered everybody.
The rule that works is this. For each way the electron can go, there's a number. We call it an amplitude.
Phi one for going through hole one. Phi two for hole two.
These are complex numbers, little arrows if you like, with a length and a direction.
When there are two ways it can happen, and you don't know which, you add the arrows.
And then the probability is the length of the total arrow, squared.
If the arrows point the same way, you get a big answer. If they point opposite, they cancel, and you get nothing.
That's all there is to it. That's the rule. Nobody has found a deeper one.
Now, you say, wait a minute. Each electron must go through one hole or the other.
Let's just look and see which one it goes through.
So we put a light behind the wall. When an electron goes by, it scatters some light, and we see a flash at hole one or at hole two.
And sure enough, every time, we see a flash at one hole or the other. Never both. Never half.
So we sort the clicks. The ones that went through hole one give P one. Hole two gives P two.
And the total, when we're watching? It's P one plus P two. The interference is gone.
Turn off the light, and the wiggles come back.
So the electron behaves differently when we look at it.
Well, maybe our light is too strong. It knocks the electron around.
So let's make it gentler. Make the light dimmer.
But light comes in lumps too, photons. Dimmer light means fewer photons, not softer ones.
So sometimes the electron goes by and we miss it. No flash at all.
The ones we saw make P one plus P two. The ones we missed make interference.
Use longer wavelength light, so each photon gives a softer kick. Then the flash is so blurry you can't tell which hole it came from.
Right when you lose the ability to say which hole, the interference comes back.
Nature is very careful. You can never have both the which-way information and the wiggles.
This is the uncertainty principle at work.
It's not that our instruments are clumsy. Any way you could possibly find out which hole the electron went through will destroy the pattern.
If it were possible to beat this, the whole of quantum mechanics would fall apart. Nobody has ever found a way.
So what do we know? We know how to calculate. Add the amplitudes for the ways you can't tell apart, then square.
If you can tell them apart, even in principle, add the probabilities instead.
And can we say how it really works underneath? What the machinery is? No.
We can only predict the odds. That's the best physics can do right now, and maybe it's the way nature is.
It's strange. But that's the way it is. And it agrees with every experiment ever done.
Next time, we'll start using these amplitudes for real.
